Far from being an overreach, this measure is a necessary and just safeguard for the preservation of the nation’s values, sovereignty, and safety.

National Security Demands Accountability

The most compelling argument for expanding revocation authority lies in the imperative of national security. The United States has repeatedly confronted cases where naturalized citizens have engaged in activities that pose existential threats to the country. The 2013 Boston Marathon bombing, perpetrated by Dzhokhar and Tamerlan Tsarnaev—one of whom was a naturalized citizen—serves as a stark reminder of this vulnerability. While Dzhokhar Tsarnaev was eventually convicted and sentenced to death, his status as a U.S. citizen complicated legal proceedings and underscored a critical flaw: even those who commit heinous acts against the nation retain the full rights and protections of citizenship. This is not an isolated incident. In 2016, a naturalized citizen, Nidal Hasan, carried out the Fort Hood massacre, killing 13 people in an act of domestic terrorism. Such cases demonstrate that the current system lacks an effective mechanism to strip citizenship from those who have demonstrated a clear and present danger to the United States.

Moreover, the threat landscape has evolved significantly in the 21st century. Cyber espionage, foreign influence operations, and lone-wolf terrorism have become increasingly prevalent, often involving naturalized citizens with ties to adversarial nations. For example, in 2020, a naturalized U.S. citizen was charged with acting as an unregistered agent of the Chinese government, engaging in espionage activities that compromised national security. Under the current legal framework, such individuals can be prosecuted for their crimes but cannot have their citizenship revoked, despite their clear betrayal of the nation. Expanding the grounds for revocation would provide a critical tool to remove such threats, while also serving as a powerful deterrent. If naturalized citizens know that engaging in acts of disloyalty or serious criminality could result in the loss of their citizenship—and potential deportation—they may be less inclined to engage in such activities in the first place. In an era where national security threats are increasingly complex and decentralized, the ability to revoke citizenship is not just a punitive measure but a proactive one, designed to protect the nation from within.

Citizenship as a Social Contract

At its core, citizenship is a social contract—a mutually beneficial agreement between an individual and the nation. In exchange for the rights and protections of citizenship, individuals pledge their loyalty, obedience to the law, and a commitment to the nation’s values. For naturalized citizens, this contract is particularly explicit. During the naturalization ceremony, they take an Oath of Allegiance, swearing to "support and defend the Constitution and laws of the United States of America against all enemies, foreign and domestic," and to "bear true faith and allegiance to the same." This oath is not a mere formality; it is the foundation of the citizen-state relationship. When a naturalized citizen violates this oath through criminal activity or acts of disloyalty, they breach the very contract that granted them the privileges of citizenship.

The principle of conditional citizenship is already embedded in U.S. law. Permanent residents (green card holders) can be deported for certain crimes, demonstrating that residency—and by extension, citizenship—is not an absolute right but a conditional privilege. Similarly, current law allows for denaturalization if it is proven that an individual obtained citizenship through fraud or misrepresentation (8 U.S.C. § 1451). Expanding this principle to include post-naturalization acts that demonstrate a fundamental breach of loyalty is a logical and necessary extension. If a naturalized citizen engages in treason, espionage, or violent crimes against the state, they have effectively renounced the responsibilities that come with citizenship. The nation, in turn, should have the right to revoke the privileges that accompany it.

Some may argue that birthright citizens can also commit acts of disloyalty, yet their citizenship cannot be revoked. However, this comparison falters on both legal and philosophical grounds. Birthright citizenship is conferred by the Fourteenth Amendment, which guarantees citizenship to all persons "born or naturalized in the United States." The Supreme Court has consistently held that birthright citizenship cannot be revoked without due process, as it is a constitutional right. Naturalized citizenship, on the other hand, is a statutory privilege granted by Congress under its naturalization powers (Article I, Section 8 of the Constitution). As such, it is inherently conditional. The distinction between birthright and naturalized citizenship is not a form of discrimination but a recognition of the different legal and philosophical foundations upon which each is granted.

Historical and Legal Precedent

The idea that citizenship can be revoked for disloyalty or criminal activity is not a radical departure from existing law but rather a return to historical precedent. The United States has a long, if contentious, history of denaturalizing individuals who have betrayed the nation. During World War II, the U.S. government revoked the citizenship of individuals who had obtained it fraudulently or who engaged in activities supporting enemy nations. In Kawakita v. United States (1952), the Supreme Court upheld the denaturalization of Tomoya Kawakita, a Japanese-American dual citizen who had been convicted of treason for his actions as a prisoner-of-war camp guard during the war. While the legal landscape has shifted since then—particularly with the Supreme Court’s 1967 decision in Afroyim v. Rusk, which limited the government’s ability to revoke citizenship for certain acts—these historical cases demonstrate that the principle of conditional citizenship is deeply rooted in American jurisprudence.

More recently, the U.S. has continued to use denaturalization as a tool to combat fraud and national security threats. In 2020, the Department of Justice established the Denaturalization Section within its Civil Division, which has since pursued cases against individuals who lied on their naturalization applications, particularly those with ties to terrorism or human rights abuses. For example, in 2018, a federal court revoked the citizenship of a former Nazi guard who had concealed his wartime activities when applying for naturalization. These cases demonstrate that denaturalization is a viable and necessary tool for maintaining the integrity of the citizenship process. Expanding this authority to include post-naturalization acts of disloyalty or serious criminality would align with this historical and legal tradition, ensuring that citizenship remains a privilege reserved for those who uphold its responsibilities.

Furthermore, the U.S. is not alone in recognizing the principle of conditional citizenship. Many nations, including the United Kingdom, Canada, and Australia, have laws allowing for the revocation of citizenship from naturalized individuals who engage in terrorism, treason, or other serious crimes. For instance, the UK’s Immigration Act of 2014 grants the Home Secretary the power to strip citizenship from dual nationals (including naturalized citizens) if it is "conducive to the public good." These laws have been upheld by courts as a necessary measure to protect national security. If other democratic nations recognize the need for conditional citizenship, there is no reason the United States should not do the same.

Addressing Counterarguments

Critics of expanding revocation authority raise several valid concerns, including potential violations of due process, the creation of a two-tiered system of citizenship, and the risk of government abuse. However, these objections can be addressed through careful legal and procedural safeguards.

Due Process and Fairness

One of the most common criticisms is that revoking citizenship without robust due process protections would violate the Constitution. However, this concern is misplaced. The current denaturalization process already includes extensive due process protections, such as the right to a fair hearing, legal representation, and the opportunity to appeal. Any expansion of revocation authority would—and must—maintain these safeguards. Revocation would not be an administrative action taken lightly but a judicial process requiring clear and convincing evidence of disloyalty or criminal activity. The burden of proof would rest with the government, ensuring that individuals are not arbitrarily stripped of their citizenship. In this way, revocation would function similarly to other serious legal penalties, such as deportation or felony disenfranchisement, which also require due process.

The Myth of a Two-Tiered System

Another objection is that expanding revocation authority would create a two-tiered system of citizenship, where naturalized citizens are treated as second-class. However, this argument ignores the fundamental legal distinction between birthright and naturalized citizenship. Birthright citizenship is a constitutional right, guaranteed by the Fourteenth Amendment, and cannot be revoked without a constitutional amendment. Naturalized citizenship, by contrast, is a statutory privilege granted by Congress. This distinction is not a form of discrimination but a recognition of the different legal foundations of each type of citizenship. Just as permanent residents can be deported for certain crimes, naturalized citizens can have their citizenship revoked for breaches of the social contract. This is not a two-tiered system but a coherent legal framework that reflects the conditional nature of naturalized citizenship.

Moreover, the idea that naturalized citizens are somehow less deserving of protection is a strawman. The vast majority of naturalized citizens are law-abiding, patriotic individuals who contribute immensely to the nation. Expanding revocation authority is not about targeting immigrants but about holding all citizens—naturalized or otherwise—accountable for their actions. The focus is on the act, not the individual. If a naturalized citizen commits treason or engages in terrorism, they have forfeited their right to the privileges of citizenship, just as a birthright citizen who commits such acts would forfeit their freedom through imprisonment.

Preventing Abuse and Arbitrariness

A third concern is that expanding revocation authority could lead to government abuse, particularly against minority or immigrant communities. This is a serious concern, given the history of discriminatory immigration policies in the United States. However, it is one that can be mitigated through clear legal standards and judicial oversight. Grounds for revocation should be narrowly defined to include only the most serious offenses, such as:

  • Treason or espionage (e.g., providing material support to a foreign adversary);
  • Terrorism or violent extremism (e.g., participation in or support for designated terrorist organizations);
  • ** Serious felonies against the state** (e.g., sedition, insurrection, or large-scale fraud against the government);
  • Acts of foreign allegiance (e.g., fighting for a foreign military hostile to the U.S. or holding office in a foreign government without renouncing U.S. citizenship).

Additionally, revocation should require a high burden of proof, such as clear and convincing evidence, and should be subject to judicial review. By limiting the grounds for revocation to egregious acts that demonstrate a clear breach of loyalty, the risk of arbitrary or discriminatory application can be significantly reduced.Furthermore, to prevent statelessness—a concern under international law—revocation should only apply to individuals who hold dual citizenship or who are eligible for citizenship in another country. The U.S. already follows this principle in existing denaturalization cases, and it can be extended to new grounds for revocation.

The Moral and Practical Imperative

Beyond the legal and security arguments, there is a moral imperative to expand revocation authority. Citizenship is not merely a legal status but a profound commitment to a shared set of values, including loyalty, responsibility, and respect for the rule of law. When an individual voluntarily chooses to become a U.S. citizen, they are not just gaining rights but also accepting duties—the duty to uphold the Constitution, to defend the nation, and to contribute to its well-being. If an individual violates these duties in a fundamental way, the nation has not only the right but the obligation to respond.

From a practical standpoint, expanding revocation authority would also align with public sentiment. Polls consistently show that Americans view citizenship as a privilege that should be earned and maintained. A 2021 Pew Research Center survey found that 74% of Americans believe that immigrants should be required to demonstrate a commitment to American values as part of the naturalization process. Extending this principle to post-naturalization behavior is a natural progression. Furthermore, revocation would serve as a deterrent, discouraging naturalized citizens from engaging in criminal or disloyal activities. In the same way that the threat of imprisonment deterrs crime, the threat of losing citizenship could deter acts of betrayal.

Some may argue that revocation is an extreme measure, but it is important to remember that citizenship is the most fundamental legal tie between an individual and the nation. If that tie is severed through deliberate and serious misconduct, the consequences should be proportional. Revocation is not about punishment for its own sake but about preserving the integrity of citizenship and protecting the nation from those who seek to harm it from within.

Conclusion: Reaffirming the Sanctity of Citizenship

The proposal to expand the U.S. government’s authority to revoke naturalized citizenship for criminal activity or acts of disloyalty is not a call for draconian measures but a reaffirmation of the principles that underpin citizenship itself. Citizenship is a privilege, not an entitlement, and it comes with responsibilities as well as rights. When those responsibilities are flagrantly violated, the nation must have the means to respond.

Expanding revocation authority would strengthen national security by removing threats from within, uphold the social contract between the nation and its citizens, and align U.S. law with historical precedent and international norms. It would also send a clear message to all citizens—naturalized or birthright—that loyalty and adherence to the law are not optional but essential components of membership in the American community.

To be sure, any expansion of revocation authority must be implemented with care, ensuring that due process is respected, abuse is prevented, and the grounds for revocation are narrowly tailored to the most serious offenses. But these challenges are not insurmountable. With the right legal frameworks and safeguards in place, the United States can take a necessary step toward protecting its sovereignty, its values, and its people.

In the end, the question is not whether the U.S. can expand its authority to revoke naturalized citizenship but whether it can afford not to. In a world where threats to national security are increasingly complex and where the bonds of citizenship are tested daily, the answer is clear: the time has come to make naturalized citizenship explicitly conditional, ensuring that those who betray the nation forfeit their place within it. Only then can the United States truly safeguard the integrity of its citizenship and the security of its people.

Expanding the government’s authority to revoke naturalized citizenship for post-naturalization criminal or disloyal conduct is not only justified but essential for protecting national security, preserving the integrity of citizenship, and ensuring that the social contract between the state and its citizens remains inviolable.

National Security Imperative

The foremost argument for expanding denaturalization authority lies in the imperative of national security. The United States faces an array of threats, both foreign and domestic, from individuals who may exploit the privileges of citizenship to harm the country. Naturalized citizens who engage in terrorism, espionage, or other acts of disloyalty pose a unique danger: they enjoy the full rights and freedoms of citizenship, including the ability to travel freely, access sensitive information, and influence political processes. For instance, in recent years, several naturalized citizens have been implicated in plots to support terrorist organizations like ISIS or to leak classified information to adversarial nations. If such individuals retain their U.S. citizenship, they cannot be deported and may continue to pose a threat from within. Revoking their citizenship and subsequently removing them from the country eliminates that threat and sends a clear message that the United States will not tolerate betrayal from those who have voluntarily joined its citizenry.

The Conditional Nature of Naturalized Citizenship

Citizenship is not merely a legal status; it is a bond of mutual commitment between the individual and the state. For native-born Americans, this bond is inherent and generally irrevocable. However, naturalized citizens make a conscious choice to become Americans, swearing an oath to “support and defend the Constitution and laws of the United States” and to “renounce and abjure all allegiance and fidelity to any foreign prince, potentate, state, or sovereignty.” By taking this oath, they enter into a contract with the nation. If they later violate that contract through serious criminal behavior or acts of disloyalty, the nation has the right—indeed, the obligation—to rescind the privileges it has granted. This conditional aspect of naturalized citizenship is rooted in the principle that privileges earned can be forfeited when the terms under which they were granted are broken. It does not create an unequal class of citizens; rather, it recognizes the unique circumstances under which naturalized citizens acquire their status.

Deterrence and Upholding the Integrity of Citizenship

Expanding denaturalization authority would also serve as a powerful deterrent against post-naturalization misconduct. Knowing that citizenship could be lost for engaging in activities that harm the country would encourage naturalized citizens to uphold their oath with the utmost seriousness. Moreover, it would reinforce the integrity of the citizenship process itself. Citizenship is a precious and hard-earned privilege; allowing individuals to retain it after betraying the nation devalues that privilege for all who have obtained it lawfully and loyally. Just as a felon may lose the right to vote or bear arms, a naturalized citizen who commits egregious offenses against the country should face the ultimate consequence: loss of the right to call themselves an American. This not only punishes the offender but also reaffirms the high standards expected of those who join the American family by choice.

International Precedents and Compatibility with Democratic Values

The United States need not venture into uncharted territory in adopting such a policy. Many of its closest allies have long had provisions for revoking citizenship in cases of serious criminal or disloyal conduct. The United Kingdom can strip citizenship from naturalized persons if it is “conducive to the public good,” often applied to terrorists and traitors. Canada allows revocation for fraud, misrepresentation, or knowingly concealing material circumstances, and has considered extending it to acts of terrorism. Australia can revoke citizenship for dual nationals who engage in terrorist activities. France, Germany, and the Netherlands have similar mechanisms. These democracies recognize that the safety of the nation sometimes necessitates the revocation of citizenship from those who abuse it. The United States, as a global leader in the fight against terrorism and transnational crime, should align itself with these international norms, ensuring it has all necessary tools to protect its interests.

Safeguards and Fairness: Addressing Legitimate Concerns

Critics of expanded denaturalization often raise valid concerns about due process, potential discrimination, and the risk of statelessness. These concerns can be addressed through carefully crafted legislation that includes robust safeguards. First, revocation should be limited to the most serious offenses: acts of terrorism, espionage, treason, taking up arms against the United States, or other felonies that directly threaten national security or public safety. Second, the process must be judicial, requiring proof beyond a reasonable doubt in a federal court, with all the protections of the legal system. Third, to avoid statelessness—a condition that international law generally condemns—revocation should only apply if the individual holds or is eligible for another citizenship, or if they would not be rendered stateless by the action. This mirrors the approach taken by other nations and respects human rights. Fourth, clear statutory criteria and oversight mechanisms can prevent misuse for political or discriminatory purposes. With these safeguards, the expanded authority would be both fair and effective.

Refuting Counterarguments

Some argue that allowing denaturalization for post-naturalization conduct creates a two-tiered system of citizenship, where naturalized citizens are treated as second-class. This objection misunderstands the nature of the social contract. Native-born citizens acquire their status by birth, without any choice or oath; naturalized citizens, by contrast, voluntarily assume the obligations of citizenship. It is entirely reasonable that violating those obligations could lead to loss of status, whereas native-born citizens, who never made such a voluntary commitment, are not subject to the same conditionality. This distinction is not invidious; it is a logical consequence of the different paths to citizenship.

Serious criminal or disloyal acts—such as treason or fighting for an enemy—can be construed as a voluntary abandonment of one’s oath, thus constituting implied renunciation. Congress already has the power to define expatriating acts under 8 U.S.C. § 1481; expanding that list to include such egregious conduct would be consistent with the constitutional framework. Finally, concerns about discouraging naturalization are misplaced. The prospect of losing citizenship for betraying the country is not a burden but a reminder of the solemn responsibility that comes with being an American. Those who genuinely wish to contribute to the nation and abide by its laws have nothing to fear. In fact, such a policy may enhance public confidence in the naturalization process, reassuring citizens that the government is committed to ensuring that only loyal individuals retain the full benefits of membership.

Conclusion

Expanding the U.S. government’s authority to revoke naturalized citizenship from individuals who engage in criminal or disloyal acts is a necessary and justified measure. It strengthens national security, upholds the conditional nature of the social contract for naturalized citizens, deters misconduct, and brings the United States in line with its allies. With appropriate safeguards to protect due process and prevent statelessness, this expansion of authority would provide a vital tool for protecting the nation’s interests while preserving the integrity of American citizenship. The time has come for Congress to enact legislation that reflects these principles and ensures that those who betray the trust placed in them do not continue to enjoy the privileges of being an American.

It is time to close this dangerous loophole. Naturalized citizenship should be a conditional privilege, not an irrevocable right. The safety of the American people—not abstract ideals of unlimited belonging—must come first.
